entry.title: LensSimulator.photo: free bokeh and lens simulator
entry.summary: 1 minute read Peter Wey's free lens simulator compares focal lengths, apertures, sensor formats, and bokeh side by side. Its ray-traced profiles include Nikon, Canon, Sony, and even the Helios 44-2. If you're looking to while away some time over the Thanksgiving weekend in the US
entry.content:
1 minute read

Peter Wey's free lens simulator compares focal lengths, apertures, sensor formats, and bokeh side by side. Its ray-traced profiles include Nikon, Canon, Sony, and even the Helios 44-2.

If you're looking to while away some time over the Thanksgiving weekend in the US, or just trying to take shelter from the Black Friday lunacy that now seems to have spread everywhere else, you could do worse than visit LensSimulator.photo.

Developed by Peter Wey, it's a free browser tool for comparing focal length, aperture, sensor format, depth of field, and bokeh across two side-by-side setups.

How the ray-traced lens profiles work

The picture is ray-traced through a 3D scene, and you can choose between an ideal thin lens and a profile that traces rays through the glass, aperture stop, and focusing groups. Rays accumulate over time, so the image cleans up the longer you leave it.

The site lists 287 profiles, which it says are ray-traced from real lens patents. Nikon leads with 86, followed by Canon with 58, Fujifilm with 41, Leica with 38, and Sony with 35. The list also takes in the likes of Sigma, Samyang, Viltrox, Angénieux, Zeiss, and Helios, with older glass such as the Helios 44-2 and Kodak Aero Ektar in the mix.

According to the site, the traced profiles model distortion, vignetting, color fringing, aperture blade shape, cat's-eye highlights, spherical aberration, and focus breathing. An Optical X-Ray view shows a cross-section of the lens, along with the aperture stop, ray path, and focusing groups.

Sensor options run from 1-inch through Micro Four Thirds, APS-C, full frame, and digital medium format to 4x5 and 8x10. Focal lengths extend from 8mm to 800mm, with apertures from f/0.95 to f/32.

What it can't do

The site is also upfront about what's missing. Flare, ghosting, coatings, assembly tolerances, sample variation, aspherical molding texture, and sensor noise are all absent from the model. It also warns that a profile follows its patent, which may differ from the lens that went on sale, and that patent-based bokeh can differ from the retail product, especially at close focus. Slider values are nominal, and the lens entries aren't sharpness rankings.

In short, LensSimulator.photo is no replacement for a lens test, but it could help you work out what you want to test when you get to that stage. It's also admirably free and available in 10 languages.

entry.title: US tariffs 2026: what they mean for camera kit
entry.summary: 3 minute read US tariffs 2026: what they mean for camera kit 5:27 The US has proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including major sources of camera kit. Many increases look smaller than advertised. For now. Here we go again. The US has proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, inclu
entry.content:
3 minute read
US tariffs 2026: what they mean for camera kit
5:27

The US has proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including major sources of camera kit. Many increases look smaller than advertised. For now.

Here we go again. The US has proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including several that matter for camera and production kit. However, for many importers the extra hit would be much smaller than the headline numbers suggest. For now, at least.

As if the ongoing rumbling of RAMageddon and sweeping manufacturer price rises weren’t bad enough, tariffs are back. Strictly speaking, we are well past part 2 by now, but then this franchise has never worried much about such niceties as continuity or even logic.

The good news, relatively speaking, is that the proposed increases are in many cases a lot smaller than the headline rates suggest, because the new figures absorb some tariffs already in place. The less good news is that they could still go higher.

This is where we are. On November 25, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed a new round of duties on 14 economies. It follows an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act into what the US calls structural excess capacity in manufacturing: in essence, some countries are making too much stuff. And if you think that sounds like a fairly bullshit reason, you’re not wrong. The move is part of the US administration’s effort to rebuild the global tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February, and it is combing the country’s labyrinthine trade legislation for any small print or loophole that will get the job done.

The list includes China, the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia, along with Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Singapore, and Switzerland. The UK is not on it, and USTR has yet to make a determination on Mexico or Norway. Canada, source of much tariff-related presidential ire in recent months, wasn’t part of this investigation.

These are proposals, and none of the new duties is in force yet. But a lot of these countries have at least something to do with camera manufacture. Some have even been where camera vendors have moved facilities partly in response to US-China tensions.

Adding up the numbers

The main proposal is 15% for the EU, and up to 15% for Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan. Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia face up to 18%. China faces up to 20% on many goods, with different treatment for products listed in annexes, while Vietnam faces up to 35%, which could be adjusted to 20% if it reaches a trade agreement.

Crucially, these figures cannot simply be added to existing bills. As law firm Wiley explains, the new duties will largely top up July's forced labor tariffs (though there are different rules for some Chinese goods).

For products already paying the July tariff, the maximum increase under the main proposal would be around 2.5 percentage points for Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland, and 5 points for the EU and Taiwan. For Thailand it would be 5.5 points, for China goods outside the annexes 7.5, and for Malaysia and Indonesia 8. Vietnam is the outlier at up to 22.5 points, though this could fall to 7.5 if it reaches the aforementioned trade agreement.

Wiggle room for more rises

A smaller increase is still an increase. For Japanese kit already paying the July tariff, another 2.5% on a $2000 customs value means up to $50 more in duty. And there is a potential sting in the tail here too. USTR has also set out higher rates for some economies if trade commitments prove “unsatisfactory”. These include up to 40% for China, up to 25% for South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia, and up to 20% for the EU and Japan. And we’ve yet to see a clear test for what counts as unsatisfactory.

There are exemptions for each country. In Japan’s case, we found no annex listing for the main camera headings or camera lenses, and many other relevant-looking entries are limited to civil aircraft use. Solid-state storage, flat panel display modules, and one category of computer-type monitor are listed without that restriction.

The pushback has already started. Japan has protested to the US over the plans, while the European Commission strongly rejects the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. It also expects any resulting measure to respect the trade deal struck in 2025.

What happens next?

The can has now been firmly kicked into the new year. Written comments and requests to appear at the hearings are due by January 5, 2027, with hearings scheduled to start on January 25. There is no date for the new tariffs to take effect, but it’s worth noting that the current US-China trade truce is due to expire on January 10.

So the sequel may be less frightening than its poster suggests, at least on the main proposed rates. But with Democrats having won Congress, we wouldn’t be surprised to see a lame duck president turn increasingly to the world stage to make his mark, or vent his frustrations. There’s definitely room yet for this to turn into a horror movie.

entry.content:
3 minute read

Aiarty Video Enhancer bundles three AI models for noisy, soft, and low-resolution footage. The Lifetime License is $129 for Black Friday, down from $235.

[Sponsored article]

The standard advice for bad footage is to shoot it again, but that only goes so far and is not always possible. That does nothing for a wedding that only happened once, a decade of archive clips, or a client's low-resolution master that has to run on a 4K screen next week. Software repair is often the only option, and the sensible way to approach it is the way a medic would with any patient who comes through the ER doors: diagnose first, then pick the treatment.

Aiarty Video Enhancer is built around that idea of triage. It is a Windows and macOS application that bundles three AI models. Each is aimed at a different kind of damage, and frame interpolation, audio cleanup, and basic finishing tools round out the package.

Aiarty is running a Black Friday sale on its Lifetime License. The Lifetime License is a one-time purchase at $129, down from $235 (45% off). It covers up to three Windows PCs or three Macs, includes unlimited free updates, and comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee. Alternatively, a 1-Year License is available for $79 (regularly $99). You can choose the license plan based on personal demand.

Diagnosis: what is wrong with the clip?

Footage usually fails in one of five ways, and Aiarty's tools map onto these failures.

Footage problem

Where Aiarty points you

Typical material

Noise and grain from high ISO or low light

superVideo vHQ, plus the video denoising controls

Receptions, indoor events, night streets

Mild softness or general degradation

Smooth-HQ v3

Handheld clips, slight focus misses, lens softness

Lost texture in skin, hair, or foliage

moDetail-HQ v3

Interviews, travel, and nature footage

Too little resolution for a 4K timeline

Upscaling to 4K, with the model matched to the content

Older 1080p projects, archived DSLR clips

Choppy motion

Frame interpolation, up to 120 fps

Sports, action, wildlife, slow-motion sources

Different AI tools are trained in different ways and have different strengths and weaknesses. Aiarty offers three models: moDetail-HQ v3 is the detail specialist, Smooth-HQ v3 is the natural-looking general repair option, and superVideo vHQ is the heavy-duty choice for noisy, low-light, or badly degraded material.

A strength slider sets how hard the AI works, so you can pull back if a result starts to look processed. The company says the aim is to avoid the over-smoothed, plastic look that aggressive noise reduction can produce. Aiarty's demo clips below show the effect.

Four before-and-after demos

Here are four brief demonstration videos covering the main repair jobs, showing what the software can do. Given that all this is possible with a $129 Lifetime License on the Black Friday deal, it's impressive stuff.

Remove noise from low-light video

Unblur a cropped clip and make video clearer

 

Restore old footage

 

Upscale for 4K quality

 

Color, HDR, audio, and editing tools

Four extra tools sit alongside the main enhancement engine:

  • Color adjustment covers brightness, contrast, saturation, exposure, highlights, and shadows.
  • SDR-to-HDR conversion offers adjustable enhancement modes.
  • Audio denoising reduces background noise to improve vocal clarity.
  • Basic editing handles crop, rotate, flip, trim, and deinterlace.

These are extremely useful tools that can save a round trip when a clip only needs a quick fix before it moves on to a grading suite or NLE. Get the $129 Lifetime License Black Friday deal while it lasts >>

Where the processing happens

Footage is processed on your own computer rather than uploaded to cloud servers. This matters if you handle client material or unreleased work. The software uses GPU acceleration, with two modes to tune it. Turbo Mode prioritizes faster processing time, and Step Mode reduces VRAM requirements for machines with less graphics memory. Batch processing queues multiple clips, so a back catalog can run unattended.

The workflow is short: import clips, choose a model and settings, preview and adjust the strength, then export one clip or a whole batch. Defaults suit first-time users, and every parameter is adjustable.

Limits worth understanding

AI repair can only work with what the source holds. Interpolated frames are generated rather than captured, and heavily damaged footage will give more variable results than a clip that is merely soft. Performance also depends on your hardware, which is the reason Turbo and Step Modes exist. Test a representative clip on your own machine, check the output at full size, and choose the model and strength from there.

Black Friday pricing and system requirements

The Lifetime License is $129, down from $235 (45% off). The Lifetime License is a single payment that activates on up to three Windows PCs or three Macs, includes unlimited free updates, and comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee. The 1-Year License covers one computer and one year of updates and is $79, down from $99. Minimum requirements are Windows 10 (x64), version 1809 or later (1903 or later for GPU acceleration), or macOS 13.0 or later.

Aiarty's Image Enhancer for stills is also on sale, as we covered in October.

To return to the theme of medicine that we started here with the concept of triage, progress in this area has been astounding in recent years. Some clips can be saved nowadays that you would never have given the chance only a few years ago. If you have a clip that has been sitting on a drive because it never looked good enough, the Black Friday offer is the easiest route to finding out whether it can be restored to its former glory.

entry.summary: 1 minute read TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH: price and specs 2:14 TTArtisan's AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH is a full-frame ultra-wide prime for Sony E and Nikon Z. It costs $489, though older Sony bodies have limited support. TTArtisan has added a 12mm to its growing line of budget autofocu
entry.content:
1 minute read
TTArtisan AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH: price and specs
2:14

TTArtisan's AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH is a full-frame ultra-wide prime for Sony E and Nikon Z. It costs $489, though older Sony bodies have limited support.

TTArtisan has added a 12mm to its growing line of budget autofocus primes. The AF 12mm f/2.8 ASPH covers full frame and is listed for Sony E and Nikon Z mounts at $489.

At 122°, this is properly wide, which suits interiors, architecture, and gimbal work.

Autofocus options at this focal length are still few, which explains why the announcement is getting a decent amount of traction online. The lens uses an STM stepping motor, with eye- and face-detection tracking claimed by the company.

Specs, size, and filter support

The optical formula runs to 16 elements in 10 groups, including two aspherical elements. The aperture runs from f/2.8 to f/16, with six blades and a clicked ring, and the lens focuses down to 0.18 m (7.1 in).

The lens has an 82 mm filter thread, and TTArtisan includes a metal filter holder for standard 82 mm filters, plus a metal cap and hood. Weight is listed as between 336 and 349 g (11.9 to 12.3 oz), which is light for a lens this wide.

TTArtisan's own claims include excellent aberration and distortion control, sharpness from center to edge, minimal focus breathing, and six-point sunstars when stopped down.

Sony E compatibility varies by camera body

Anyone interested needs to pay attention to compatibility, especially for video. TTArtisan says the lens works seamlessly on Nikon Z bodies, but older Sony E cameras have limited functionality. The a7 III is fully compatible for photo modes and only partially for video, and the original a7 and a7 II lack full compatibility. AF performance may be limited on some bodies, with firmware updates in development for others. Full details are on TTArtisan's product page.

Pricing and availability

The lens is available to preorder now at $489 in both mounts. One caption on the product page references an L-Mount version, but as yet there is no official word on its status.

entry.title: Insta360 Ace Pro 3 launch date: December 1 confirmed
entry.summary: 2 minute read Insta360 Ace Pro 3 launch date: December 1 confirmed 3:23 Insta360 will unveil the Ace Pro 3 in China on December 1. Its teaser points to interchangeable lenses, a variable aperture, and focus control. Well, this is a surprise. In the high-stakes game of next-genera
entry.content:
2 minute read
Insta360 Ace Pro 3 launch date: December 1 confirmed
3:23

Insta360 will unveil the Ace Pro 3 in China on December 1. Its teaser points to interchangeable lenses, a variable aperture, and focus control.

Well, this is a surprise. In the high-stakes game of next-generation action camera launches, which we confidently said earlier this month was on hold until next year, Insta360 has pulled the trigger on the Ace Pro 3.

Insta360's official Weibo account (weibo.com/insta360) posted a teaser video and key visual on the evening of November 24, tagged #影石acepro3# and promising an announcement on December 1 at 20:00 Beijing time (12:00 UTC). Nothing has appeared on Insta360's global channels or insta360.com yet, which might point to this being a China-only announcement with the global launch coming later, perhaps to coincide with CES 2027 (January 6 to 9).

Insta360 and DJI both used this tactic during the long, drawn-out launches of the Luna and Pocket 4 series gimbal cameras. Effectively, the Chinese release provides a soft launch to the rest of the world, which the companies then circle back to with the official global launch later.

So, while the announcement is now set for December, the global rollout and availability may well slip into next year. Which, we guess, means we might have been right about the 2027 thing after all…

What the Ace Pro 3 teaser reveals

The tagline "定局已破" loosely translates as "the mold is broken", or overturning something everyone took as settled. Getting a decent-quality upload of the Weibo video isn't easy from outside China, so here's leaker Igor Bogdanov's share of it, which provides the best quality we've got so far.

👉Well, hello, @insta360 Ace Pro 3. Long time no see 🫣 https://t.co/am7X3Q8Jrn

— Igor Bogdanov (@Quadro_News) November 24, 2026

Breaking the mold seems about right. The teaser gives four clues: bokeh, variable aperture, interchangeable lenses, and focusing. Some of these have appeared on action cameras before, with the DJI Osmo Action 6 bringing a variable aperture and the GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS swappable lenses, but all four together really would be something else.

The key visual, meanwhile, shows three different lens heads: a domed element under a petal-style hood, an octagonal lens with Leica branding and a partial "ASPH." marking, and a third dome with a red accent ring.

Taken together, the clues point to a versatile all-rounder in a very compact body.

Ace Pro 3 rumored specs and price

Unsurprisingly, the rumor mill has kicked into top gear. 8K30 and 50 MP stills are being talked about fairly consistently, and the pricing mentioned is around the $549 to $599 region. This is significantly up from the $399 of the Ace Pro 2, but, given the new capabilities, is about what you'd expect.

Insta360 founder JK Liu has said on Chinese social media that the goal is that users don't need to carry a second camera with them for different tasks. If the company has nailed some of the technical challenges that come with cramming so much into a still-small form factor, they might not need to.

entry.title: Nikon ZR firmware 2.00 out now: full feature list and what is still to come
entry.summary: 3 minute read Nikon ZR firmware 2.00 out now: full feature list and what is still to come 5:53 Nikon's free ZR firmware 2.00 brings RED color science to H.265 through Log3G10. Open gate and anamorphic desqueeze are promised for 2027. After being heavily trailed and receiving as m
entry.content:
3 minute read
Nikon ZR firmware 2.00 out now: full feature list and what is still to come
5:53

Nikon's free ZR firmware 2.00 brings RED color science to H.265 through Log3G10. Open gate and anamorphic desqueeze are promised for 2027.

After being heavily trailed and receiving as many press releases as some entire cameras get, Nikon ZR firmware 2.00 is available to download from today, November 24. The headlines are that it brings RED color science to the camera's compact H.265 recordings, while also holding out the promise of more to come. Open gate recording and a desqueeze display for anamorphic lenses are not part of the update, but Nikon says both are in development for next year.

What arrives now

The main addition is Log3G10 gamma in the H.265 tone mode options, which enables recording in the REDWideGamutRGB gamut. Until now, ZR owners wanting RED's color pipeline had to shoot R3D NE, the RAW format Nikon developed to carry it. Nikon says H.265 gives smaller files while keeping substantial room for grading.

The rest of the update is workflow-focused, and none the worse for it:

  • A selectable High ISO NR level, in four settings, for Log3G10 and N-Log recording in H.265, and for N-Log in ProRes 422 HQ
  • Focus peaking while recording R3D NE with a 3D LUT applied
  • A 3D LUT can now be applied to HDMI output
  • ISO, exposure compensation, white balance, and color temperature can be assigned to the command dials in M mode, and 3D LUT/View Assist can be assigned to an Fn button
  • Updated processing that Nikon says suppresses frame-by-frame black level fluctuations, reducing flicker in dark areas

While all very welcome, it's hard not to be slightly more excited by what is promised for 2027.

Open gate and desqueeze: what Nikon has promised for 2027

Nikon said in September that it is developing firmware for open gate recording and a desqueeze display for anamorphic lenses, "with the goal of incorporating them in ZR firmware in 2027." Unfortunately, that is as specific as Nikon has been, with no indication of precisely when in 2027 or further detail about how it will all work, such as which open gate recording modes will be offered.

Nikon itself describes both as frequently requested features, and this is unsurprising. Open gate's ability to reframe post-shoot or deliver to multiple aspect ratios from one recording is almost tailor-made for modern briefs, while a desqueeze display makes working with anamorphic lenses much easier. In an ideal world, for a camera with the ambitions of the ZR, both should have been there from launch. There is speculation that the ZR's fanless body may be part of the reason open gate was missing, though Nikon has not confirmed this.

RED CONTROL apps and NIKKOR cinema lenses

Nikon also said in September that RED is updating its RED CONTROL and RED CONTROL PRO apps to add remote control of the ZR. At the time of writing, neither lists the ZR among supported cameras, though that may well change as the earth rotates and the US comes online today.

The wider RED and Nikon picture is also filling in. Nikon has nine NIKKOR Z CINEMA T1.9 VV lenses in development, starting with a 50mm. This has been a long time coming. The video below was released earlier this year and, as we noted in September, the 50mm may not arrive until around NAB 2027, never mind the following eight.

 

They will be worth waiting for, though. The lenses will have an image circle large enough to cover Nikon's full-frame sensors as well as the VistaVision (VV) format and the 40.96 mm × 21.60 mm (1.61 in × 0.85 in) image sensor of RED's V-RAPTOR [X], a first for NIKKOR lenses. They will also include an autofocus mechanism alongside manual focus control.

Firmware 2.00 is a free download from Nikon's ZR firmware page. The full changelog is below.

Full changelog from v1.11

Video Recording

  • Added [Log3G10] to the tone mode options available when video file type is set to [H.265 10-bit (MOV)].
  • 3D LUT can now be applied to video output via HDMI.
  • Focus peaking is now available when 3D LUT is set to ON.
  • Reduced noise in dark areas of videos.
  • [High ISO NR] is now available with [N-Log] tone mode when video file type is set to [H.265 10-bit (MOV)] or [ProRes 422 HQ 10-bit (MOV)].
  • Changed the following item names in Picture Controls:
    • [Cloud Picture Control] changed to [Imaging Recipe].
    • [Add Cloud Picture Control files] under [Set Picture Control] in the [VIDEO RECORDING MENU] changed to [Download Imaging Recipes].

Still Photography

  • Changed the following item names in Picture Controls:
    • [Cloud Picture Control] changed to [Imaging Recipe].
    • [Add Cloud Picture Control files] under [Set Picture Control] in the [PHOTO SHOOTING MENU] changed to [Download Imaging Recipes].

Controls

  • Made the following changes to the [CUSTOM SETTINGS MENU]:
    • Added b4 [Easy ISO].
    • Exposure compensation, ISO sensitivity, white balance, and color temperature can now be assigned to the command dials in mode M using [Command dials] > [Exposure setting] under f2 [Custom controls (shooting)] and g2 [Custom controls].
    • Added [3D LUT/View assist] as an assignable role to g2 [Custom controls].
    • Added g12 [Easy exposure compensation].

Other Changes

  • [Save] in [SETUP MENU] > [Manage user settings] is now [Edit].
  • Fixed an issue where scrolling with touch controls was not smooth when live view was zoomed in with the camera in tall orientation and [Auto-rotate pictures] set to OFF.

Changelog text: Nikon.

Understanding team communication needs in modern production

Wireless intercom systems have become essential for seamless collaboration across film production, live streaming, broadcasting, and on-site events. The market is increasingly favoring systems that are easy to deploy, cost-effective, and adaptable to varying crew sizes. When selecting a wireless intercom, key considerations include the number of team members, communication range, interference resistance, environmental noise cancellation, and overall budget.

Solidcom SE series: tailored solutions for every team size

Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 body-only version: price
1:28

A new, lower-priced version of the popular Fujifilm GFX Eterna 55 is being listed on both sides of the Atlantic.

As spotted by Fuji Rumors, B&H Photo is now listing a body-only version of the Fujifillm GFX Eterna 55 at $9999, against $16,499 for the original configuration, which is still on sale alongside it.

In the UK, CVP is taking pre-orders for the body at £9499 including VAT (£7915 ex VAT), with stock expected on November 27. CVP lists the contents as the camera body, battery, body cap, and PL mount adapter. The original package also included an LCD monitor and power adapter. The top handle is not listed in CVP's box contents either.

TheEterna 55 uses a 102 MP, 43.8 x 32.9 mm (1.72 x 1.30 in) sensor with dual base ISO of 800 and 3200, and an electronic variable ND filter covering ND0.6 to ND2.1 (roughly 2 to 7 stops). It weighs 2 kg (4.4 lb) and is IMAX-certified. It launched in September 2025 at $16,499 and £13,999.

Fujifilm has not yet commented on the new pricing, and we're not sure the missing components account for the whole $6500 difference. It's tempting to think that it's just a Black Friday deal, but the 'new item' and pre-order status suggest something a bit more permanent.

CVP though is also taking pre-orders for what it calls the Fujifilm GFX ETERNA 55 Plus at $20,199, which includes the following, so there could definitely be some repositioning underway.

entry.content:
1 minute read
Kodak SlideTag: price, specs, and tracking
1:57

Reto's Kodak SlideTag is a work of slight genius and combines a $34.99 keychain with an E Ink photo screen and Apple and Google device tracking.

Just in time for Christmas, Kodak licensee Reto, the company behind the zeitgeist-friendly hit Charmera camera, has launched the Kodak SlideTag, a clever little device that mashes together three things and thus becomes an impressive small object of desire.

It is a keychain with an AirTag-like Bluetooth tracker, it is a customizable E Ink display that will display your own photos, and it is a heady nostalgic trip for anyone who remembers the mingled joy and horror of family slide shows. It is a fourth thing as well, a blind box, but nothing's perfect.

Nine designs are available that all recreate the cardboard-and-plastic slide mounts that Kodachrome made familiar from 1935 onward and that were stored in shoeboxes under beds everywhere. They are built around a 1.54-inch, 6-color E Ink display at 240 x 240 pixels. Photos are loaded through the KODAK Memory Link app, which also handles slideshows, QR codes, and to-do lists.

The tracking works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub with an approximate range of up to 30 m (98 ft) in open air, and the tag can sound off at 75 dB to help you find it and whatever essential equipment it's attached to.

It is small and light at 39.3 x 46 x 7.58 mm (1.55 x 1.81 x 0.30 in) and 16.6 g (0.6 oz), and has an IP54 rating so it will handle splashes and dust but is not waterproof. It runs on a replaceable CR2032 coin cell.

Pricing and availability

Like the Charmera, the SlideTag is sold as a blind box, at $34.99. There are eight standard designs plus one secret edition with a 1/64 chance, while a whole set of eight is currently $210. Reto says that one of the basic editions will be replaced if the secret edition appears in the set.

entry.content:
3 minute read
OZ Racing’s Rally Legend campaign shot on Blackmagic 12K
5:49

Cinematographers Paolo Concari and Jacopo Cosmelli took two 12K Blackmagic cameras and a set of vintage Leica R lenses up the Apuan Alps for OZ Racing’s Rally Legend wheels.

[Blackmagic sent us this one in and we liked it enough that we're publishing it pretty much as is. Ed]

OZ Racing’s Rally Legend “Keep Exploring” campaign took cinematographers Paolo Concari and Jacopo Cosmelli to Tuscany’s Apuan Alps, where they used Blackmagic URSA Cine 12K LF and PYXIS 12K digital film cameras to film a Jeep Wrangler JK fitted with the Italian manufacturer’s new off-road wheels.

The commercial follows the Jeep across paved roads, dirt tracks, and rugged terrain before shifting its attention to a nature filmmaker exploring the landscape on foot.

One look, different shoots

“From a cinematographic standpoint, the challenge was to maintain strong visual consistency while constantly shifting between very different shooting situations,” says Cosmelli. “From vast Alpine landscapes to high frame rates of the wheels, and onboard footage, we had to move quickly between different focal lengths, camera movements, and points of view.”

While the PYXIS 12K was used for much of the landscape photography, close-ups, and moving shots, the URSA Cine 12K LF came into its own for the slow-motion footage of the wheels. “Having the same RGBW sensor technology in both cameras gave us excellent color detail, along with 16 stops of dynamic range,” Concari says. “It also meant the footage matched naturally, giving Cosmelli a consistent starting point and plenty of flexibility in color grading.”

The PYXIS 12K was rigged with a Blackmagic PYXIS Monitor, a Blackmagic PYXIS Pro Handle, a SmallRig Mini Matte Box, a video transmitter, and a RØDE boom mic. “Despite the additional accessories, the setup remained easy to work with, particularly for handheld shots following the protagonist on foot and during the driving sequences,” he explains.

“The URSA Cine 12K LF was equipped with the 5-inch HDR touchscreen monitor, Blackmagic URSA Cine Handle, and Blackmagic URSA Cine EVF, along with a NiSi Cinema C5 Matte Box.

Vintage Leica glass and a third camera

“We also used the Micro Studio Camera 4K G2 for the shots mounted on the Jeep and the FPV drone, where we needed something much smaller,” Concari added. “Both the URSA Cine and PYXIS were paired with vintage Leica R lenses, ranging from 19mm to 60mm Macro.

“We chose them for their organic rendering. They’re sharp without feeling overly clinical, with lovely microcontrast and natural bokeh. For the scenes where the actor leaves the Jeep and continues on foot, we mostly used the 24mm and 35mm on the PYXIS, shooting in 8K 3:2 at 25 fps. Those wider lenses gave us room to show the scale of the mountains without losing the character in the frame.”

For a scene with the actor standing close to the Jeep during the blue hour, Cosmelli switched to the 60mm Macro lens.

“We wanted to get closer to his face and pick up the smaller expressions, but we also had to be careful with the exposure,” he says. “He was standing in shade with a bright sky and mountains behind him. We shot at ISO 800 and used false color and the histogram to judge how far we could go without losing detail in his face or the highlights.”

For the automotive sequences, the URSA Cine 12K LF captured the Rally Legend wheels as the Jeep crossed water and loose terrain.

“We shot mainly handheld, although we also relied on a Manfrotto tripod for more controlled shots,” says Cosmelli. “We used the 24mm Leica R quite a bit, shooting 8K 3:2 Open Gate and switching to 2.4:1 when we wanted to go up to 224 fps.

“The water crossings were probably the trickiest because you never quite knew how the water was going to behave. The same with the dry leaves. We’d have one chance to catch it as the Jeep came through, so getting the timing right was important. Those shots were difficult to control because everything happened so quickly. Being able to push the frame rate meant we could really see what was happening around the wheels.”

Small cameras for tight spots

For onboard footage, the production used the Blackmagic Micro Studio Camera 4K G2, mounting it to the side, hood, and rear of the Jeep with Tilta suction cup mounts and a Manfrotto Super Clamp 035C. A Cinekinetic Cinesaddle was used to get the camera really low, right down beside the wheels. The team also flew the camera on a custom-built 178 mm (7 in) X4 FPV cinelifter drone, using either a Leica R 19mm lens with a Metabones adapter or a Laowa 7.5mm lens.

“The size of the Micro Studio Camera meant we could put it in places where the larger cameras wouldn’t fit,” Cosmelli concludes. “We could get right up close to the action with the camera mounted on the Jeep, then use it on the FPV drone for much wider shots, still recording Blackmagic RAW directly to a SanDisk SSD connected via USB-C in both setups.”

The team edited, graded, and delivered the campaign in DaVinci Resolve Studio.
